questions.question: What are the key elements of a UML class diagram?

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands the visual language of class diagrams, essential for communicating object-oriented designs in interviews and documentation.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing relationship arrows (especially inheritance vs interface implementation) or forgetting that class diagrams show structure, not runtime flow.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention multiplicity numbers (1..*, 0..1) on associations and explain when you'd use composition (filled diamond) versus aggregation (hollow diamond) based on lifecycle ownership.

questions.direct_answer: A UML class diagram represents classes as boxes divided into three sections: name at the top, attributes in the middle, methods at the bottom. Relationships between classes are shown using different line styles: solid arrows for inheritance, dashed arrows for interface implementation, diamonds for composition/aggregation, and plain lines for association. Visibility markers like + (public) and - (private) prefix members.

answer_sections.content: In a UML class diagram, each class is a box with three sections: name at top, attributes in the middle showing type and visibility (+ public, - private, # protected), and methods at the bottom. Relationships use different arrow types: a solid arrowhead means inheritance ('extends'), a dashed arrowhead means implements an interface. A filled diamond shows composition — the containing class owns the contained one (ParkingLot has a filled diamond to ParkingFloor). A hollow diamond shows aggregation — weaker association. In LLD interviews, you don't need perfect UML syntax, but using these conventions communicates your design clearly. The key is showing the relationships correctly.

sections.title: What a UML Class Diagram Communicates
sections.content: A **UML class diagram** is the blueprint for your object-oriented design — it shows what classes exist, what they contain, and how they relate to each other. Think of it like an architect's floor plan: you see the rooms (classes), the furniture in each room (attributes), what happens in each room (methods), and the doors connecting rooms (relationships). The diagram has two main parts: **class boxes** that show the structure of each class, and **relationship lines** that show how classes depend on, inherit from, or contain each other. In an LLD interview for a parking lot or ATM system, you'll use this notation to explain your design before writing any code. The diagram makes your design decisions visible: which classes are abstract, where you're using composition, and what the key collaborations are.

sections.title: Java Classes Represented in UML
Key Elements and Notation
content: **Class box structure**: Three horizontal sections — name (top), attributes/fields (middle), methods/operations (bottom). Name section can include <<stereotype>> labels.
**Visibility markers**: + for public, - for private, # for protected, ~ for package-private. These prefix each attribute and method.
**Inheritance arrow**: Solid line with hollow triangle pointing from subclass to parent class. Shows "is-a" relationship like Car extends Vehicle.
**Interface implementation**: Dashed line with hollow triangle pointing from implementing class to interface. Interface box has <<interface>> stereotype above the name.
**Composition diamond**: Filled black diamond on the container side, line to contained class. Lifecycle dependency — when ParkingLot dies, its ParkingFloors die too.
**Aggregation diamond**: Hollow white diamond for weaker ownership. The contained object can exist independently — like Vehicle assigned to ParkingSpot temporarily.
**Multiplicity notation**: Numbers like 1, 0..1, 1..*, * on association ends show how many instances participate. For example, ParkingFloor has 1..* ParkingSpots.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: A UML class diagram has two main parts: class boxes and relationship lines. Each class is a rectangle divided into three sections. The top section has the class name, sometimes with a label like interface in double angle brackets. The middle section lists attributes with their types, and the bottom section lists methods with return types. You put visibility symbols in front — plus for public, minus for private, hash for protected. That's the structure of individual classes. Now for relationships: inheritance is a solid line with a hollow arrow pointing from child to parent. When a class implements an interface, you use a dashed line with a hollow arrow. Composition is when one class owns another — you show it with a filled diamond on the owner's side. Aggregation is similar but the contained object can exist independently, so the diamond is hollow. Regular associations are just plain lines, often with multiplicity numbers like one-to-many or zero-to-one. The key mistake freshers make is mixing up the arrow types, especially inheritance versus interface implementation. Remember: solid for extends, dashed for implements. In an interview, don't try to draw every detail. Focus on the major classes, their important fields and methods, and the key relationships that show your design decisions. That's what the interviewer cares about.

questions.question: How do you draw a class diagram for a simple parking lot on a whiteboard?

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical ability to translate a real-world system into a class diagram on the spot, under time pressure, which is the core of LLD interview rounds.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Either drawing too many classes with every possible detail (wasting time) or drawing only entity names without showing relationships and key members.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain your design choices aloud while drawing — why Vehicle is abstract, why you chose composition for floors, and how the ticket links vehicle to spot for billing.

questions.direct_answer: Start by identifying the main entities: ParkingLot, ParkingFloor, ParkingSpot, Vehicle (with Car/Motorcycle subclasses), ParkingTicket, and a fee calculator. Draw a box for each with 3-5 key attributes and methods. Then connect them: ParkingLot contains multiple ParkingFloors (composition), each floor has multiple ParkingSpots (composition), Vehicle is abstract with inheritance arrows to concrete types, and ParkingTicket associates with Vehicle and ParkingSpot.

answer_sections.content: For a whiteboard class diagram, I start with the core entities and their relationships. I draw ParkingLot at the top with a composition arrow to ParkingFloor (filled diamond), ParkingFloor with composition to ParkingSpot. Vehicle is drawn as abstract in italics with Car and Motorcycle below it connected by inheritance arrows. ParkingTicket has association lines to both Vehicle (it references) and ParkingSpot (it's for). FeeCalculator is a separate box with dependency line from ParkingLot. I add key attributes and methods in each box, focusing on the important ones rather than being exhaustive. The diagram should tell the story of how the system works without needing explanation.

sections.title: The Whiteboard Class Diagram Process
sections.content: Drawing a class diagram on a whiteboard during an LLD interview is about showing your **design thinking process**, not creating perfect UML syntax. You have 15-20 minutes to sketch the major classes and their relationships for a parking lot system. The interviewer watches how you break down the problem: do you identify the right entities, do you show clear ownership relationships, do you use inheritance appropriately? Think of it like sketching a building's structure — you don't draw every nail and screw, but you show the load-bearing walls and how the floors connect. Start with the core entities (ParkingLot, ParkingSpot, Vehicle), add the supporting classes (Ticket, FeeCalculator), then draw the connecting lines to show how they work together. Keep the boxes large enough to write in, leave space between them for relationship lines, and be ready to erase and redraw as you refine your design based on interviewer questions.

sections.title: Parking Lot Core Classes in Java
Key Classes and Relationships
content: **ParkingLot → ParkingFloor**: Composition (filled diamond). The lot owns its floors — when you demolish the parking lot, the floors go with it. Multiplicity 1..*.
**ParkingFloor → ParkingSpot**: Also composition. Each floor owns its spots. A floor has many spots, each spot belongs to exactly one floor.
**Vehicle hierarchy**: Abstract Vehicle class with Car, Motorcycle, Truck as subclasses. Solid inheritance arrows point from each subclass to Vehicle. Shows different size requirements.
**ParkingSpot ↔ Vehicle**: Association (plain line). The spot has a reference to the current vehicle parked there, but the vehicle exists independently. Could be 0..1 vehicle per spot.
**ParkingTicket associations**: Links to both Vehicle and ParkingSpot. The ticket is the transaction record that ties a vehicle to a spot for a time period.
**FeeCalculator**: Separate utility class that ParkingTicket uses. Could be shown with a dashed dependency arrow since the ticket depends on it for calculations.
**Key attributes to show**: spotId, floorNumber, licensePlate, entryTime — just enough to make the design concrete without cluttering the diagram with getters and setters.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: I'd start by drawing the main container class, ParkingLot, in the center of the board. It has a name and a list of floors, so I'd write those as attributes. Then I'd draw ParkingFloor to the right with a composition diamond connecting them — that filled diamond shows the lot owns its floors. Each floor has a floor number and a list of spots, so I'd draw ParkingSpot next with another composition diamond. Now for the vehicles: I'd draw an abstract Vehicle class with licensePlate as an attribute, then draw Car and Motorcycle below it with solid inheritance arrows pointing up. I'd mark Vehicle as abstract by underlining or writing abstract above it. Next comes ParkingTicket — this connects a vehicle to a spot when someone parks. I'd draw it below the spot and vehicle, with plain association lines to both. The ticket needs entryTime and a method to calculate fees. I might add a FeeCalculator class if time allows, shown with a dashed dependency arrow from the ticket. The key mistake is trying to draw every possible class or every method. You don't need getters and setters on the diagram — just the interesting design decisions. Show what's abstract, what inherits, what's composition versus association. Talk through your choices as you draw: why Vehicle is abstract, why floors are owned by the lot, how the ticket ties everything together for billing. That's what shows design thinking.

questions.question: How do you show an interface and its implementations in a class diagram?

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of interface notation in UML, which is fundamental since well-designed systems use interfaces for loose coupling and dependency inversion.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using a solid line instead of dashed for interface implementation, or forgetting the <<interface>> stereotype label, making it look like a regular class.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that interfaces typically define behavior contracts (PaymentProcessor, NotificationService) and explain how this enables dependency injection in Spring applications.

questions.direct_answer: Draw the interface as a box with <<interface>> above the class name and only method signatures inside (no attributes). Each implementing class uses a dashed line with a hollow arrow pointing to the interface. If you have an abstract class, write the name in italics and use a solid line with hollow arrow for subclasses. You can mix both: an interface with multiple implementations, one of which is abstract with its own subclasses.

answer_sections.content: In UML, interfaces get the <<interface>> label in the class box and their methods are listed without implementation. A class implementing an interface uses a dashed line with a hollow triangular arrowhead pointing at the interface — it's 'realization' in UML terminology. Abstract classes have their name in italics and abstract methods in italics too. So for pricing: <<interface>> PricingStrategy has +calculateFee(Vehicle, Duration): BigDecimal. Then HourlyPricingStrategy and DailyPricingStrategy both have dashed implementation arrows to PricingStrategy. On a whiteboard I usually write <<interface>> or just 'I' prefix on the box to distinguish from concrete classes — perfect UML syntax matters less than clear communication.

sections.title: Representing Interfaces in UML
sections.content: An **interface** in UML represents a contract — a set of method signatures that implementing classes must provide. You draw it almost like a regular class box, but with two key differences: the **<<interface>>** stereotype label at the top, and the use of a **dashed line with hollow arrow** for implementation relationships. This visual distinction is crucial because it shows **design by contract**: the interface defines what a class can do, not how it does it. Think of an interface like a power outlet standard — the outlet (interface) promises certain capabilities, and any device (implementing class) that fits the plug can use it. In Java applications, especially Spring-based systems, interfaces are everywhere: repositories that abstract database access, services that define business operations, strategies that allow swapping algorithms. Abstract classes sit between interfaces and concrete classes — they can have some implementation but can't be instantiated. You show them with italicized names and solid arrows, distinguishing them from interfaces.

sections.title: Interface and Implementation in Java
Interface and Abstract Class Notation
content: **Interface stereotype**: The label <<interface>> goes inside the class name section, above the actual interface name. This immediately tells the reader it's a contract, not a concrete class.
**Dashed implementation line**: The line from implementing class to interface is dashed with a hollow triangle arrow pointing to the interface. Never use a solid line for implements.
**Interface contents**: Show only method signatures without bodies. Interfaces don't have attributes in Java (except constants, which you can show as static final). No constructors.
**Abstract class notation**: Write the class name in italics or add {abstract} after it. Abstract classes use solid inheritance arrows from their subclasses, just like regular inheritance.
**Multiple implementations**: Many classes can implement the same interface — draw separate dashed arrows from each implementer to the interface. This shows polymorphism visually.
**Mixing both**: A class can implement an interface and be abstract. You'd show the dashed line to the interface and italic name, with solid arrows from its concrete subclasses.
**Real-world naming**: Interfaces often end in -able (Comparable, Serializable) or describe services (PaymentProcessor, NotificationService). This naming appears in your UML boxes.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: To show an interface in a class diagram, I'd draw a regular class box but add the interface stereotype in double angle brackets at the top, like interface above the name. The interface box contains only method signatures — no attributes, no method bodies, because interfaces define contracts, not implementations. Then for each class that implements the interface, I'd draw a dashed line with a hollow arrow pointing from the implementing class to the interface. That dashed line is key — it's how you tell it's implements, not extends. If I had an abstract class, I'd write its name in italics and use a solid arrow from subclasses, the same as regular inheritance. You can combine these: an abstract class can implement an interface, so you'd have a dashed arrow from the abstract class to the interface, then solid arrows from concrete classes to the abstract class. In a parking lot system, you might have a FeeCalculator interface with HourlyFeeCalculator and FlatFeeCalculator implementations — two dashed arrows pointing to one interface box. The common mistake freshers make is using a solid line for implements, which makes it look like inheritance. Remember: dashed means implements, solid means extends. The reason this matters in real systems is that interfaces enable loose coupling. Your ParkingLot class can depend on the FeeCalculator interface without knowing which concrete calculator it's using. That's dependency injection, and it's how Spring works. When you draw it correctly in an interview, you're showing you understand this principle.

questions.question: How much detail should a class diagram in an LLD interview have?

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical judgment about what level of abstraction communicates design effectively in a time-constrained interview setting — shows experience thinking like a designer, not just a coder.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Either creating a nearly blank diagram with just class names and lines (too abstract) or drawing every field and method including constructors and getters (too detailed, wastes time).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explicitly state your detail level choice at the start: 'I'll show the core classes with key fields and methods, skipping standard getters to focus on design decisions.' Then deliver on that promise.

questions.direct_answer: Include all major classes that represent distinct responsibilities, show their important relationships (inheritance, composition, key associations), and list 3-5 critical attributes and methods per class — enough to convey design decisions. Skip getters, setters, utility methods, and minor helper classes. The goal is clarity about architecture, not completeness. If you're spending more than 15 minutes drawing, you have too much detail.

answer_sections.content: The rule for LLD interview diagrams: enough to communicate the design, not a complete specification. I show all major classes and their important relationships. For attributes, I include the fields that capture the key design decisions — like Vehicle having a VehicleType enum field — but not every trivial field. For methods, I show the key public APIs: ParkingLot.findAvailableSpot(), ParkingSpot.occupy() — not the private helpers or getters. The most important things to show are: inheritance hierarchies (abstract Vehicle), composition relationships (filled diamonds), and interfaces (<<interface>> labels). A good diagram tells the story of the design in 3-5 minutes of drawing. If I'm spending 15 minutes drawing, I'm being too detailed.

beats.text: An interview class diagram should communicate the design clearly in 3 to 5 minutes of drawing. It's a communication tool, not a specification.

groups.heading: Always include
groups.text: All major classes, inheritance hierarchies, composition relationships, and interfaces. These are the design decisions — they must be visible.

groups.heading: Include selectively
groups.text: Key attributes that reflect design choices (VehicleType enum field, boolean isOccupied) and key public methods (findAvailableSpot, occupy, free).

groups.heading: Skip entirely
groups.text: Getters, setters, private helpers, trivial fields. They add clutter without communicating design.

beats.text: Draw the diagram alongside your verbal explanation, not before and not after. Narrate each box and arrow as you draw it — the interviewer is following your reasoning, not just your pen.
sharp edge: if you're spending more than 10 minutes on the diagram, you're too detailed. Step back, focus on relationships and key design decisions only.

speakable_v2.cap: Show what's abstract, what's an interface, and how things compose or inherit. Skip getters and setters. A clean 5-minute diagram beats an exhaustive 15-minute one every time.

sections.title: The Right Level of Detail for LLD Interviews
sections.content: A class diagram in an LLD interview is a **communication tool**, not a code generation template. You have 15-20 minutes to show your design, so every box and line must earn its place. The interviewer wants to see **architectural decisions**: what are the main entities, how do they collaborate, where did you use abstraction, what are the key design patterns? Think of it like explaining a building's structure — you'd show the foundation, walls, and roof, not every nail and wire. Include details that reveal **design choices**: if ParkingSpot has a VehicleType field, that's worth showing because it drives the matching logic. But getters and setters for every field? That's assumed, skip them. Constructors? Only if they do something interesting beyond assigning fields. The balance is: enough detail that someone could understand your design and start implementing it, but not so much that the diagram becomes a wall of text. When in doubt, ask yourself: does this detail help explain a design decision, or is it mechanical boilerplate?

sections.title: Step 1: Identify Core Classes First
sections.content: Start by listing the **main entities** from the problem domain — these are your primary classes. For a parking lot: ParkingLot, ParkingFloor, ParkingSpot, Vehicle, ParkingTicket are core. For an ATM: ATM, Account, Transaction, Card, Cash are core. These classes represent distinct responsibilities and will have relationships between them. Draw these first, using most of your whiteboard space. Each core class should show 3-5 **key attributes** — the fields that drive the business logic. For ParkingSpot: spotId, type (compact/large), isOccupied, currentVehicle. Skip createdDate, lastModifiedDate, auditLog — those are infrastructure concerns, not design decisions. Then add 2-4 **important methods** — the operations that show how the class fulfills its responsibility. For ParkingSpot: assignVehicle(), releaseVehicle(), isAvailableFor(VehicleType). Don't add getSpotId(), setSpotId() — those are assumed. The core classes form the skeleton of your design.

sections.title: Step 2: Show Critical Relationships and Patterns
sections.content: Next, draw the **relationship lines** that show how classes work together. Focus on relationships that reveal design decisions. **Composition** (filled diamond) shows ownership — ParkingLot owns ParkingFloors, which is a structural choice. **Inheritance** (solid arrow) shows abstraction — Vehicle is abstract with Car/Motorcycle subclasses, which enables polymorphism. **Interfaces** (dashed arrow) show contracts — if you have a FeeCalculator interface, that's a strategy pattern that deserves visibility. Add **multiplicity** where it clarifies the model: 1..* floors per lot, 1 vehicle per occupied spot. Skip relationships that are implied or minor — you don't need to show that every class might use a Logger utility. If you're applying a **design pattern** (Strategy, Factory, Observer), make sure the diagram clearly shows it: the interface, the implementing variants, the context that uses them. These patterns are what distinguish a thoughtful design from a data model, so they justify the detail.

sections.title: Detail Level Guidelines
content: **Include major classes**: All entities with distinct responsibilities (ParkingLot, Vehicle, Ticket). Aim for 5-10 classes total in a 20-minute interview.
**Show key attributes**: Fields that drive business logic (spotType, entryTime, licensePlate). 3-5 per class. Skip audit fields, IDs unless they're meaningful.
**Include important methods**: Operations that reveal behavior (calculateFee, findAvailableSpot, park). 2-4 per class. Never show getters/setters unless they have special logic.
**Skip utility classes**: Don't draw Logger, DateUtils, StringHelper. These clutter the diagram without adding design insight. Mention them verbally if asked.
**Emphasize design patterns**: If you're using Strategy, Factory, Observer — make those visible. Show the interface, the variants, the relationships that implement the pattern.
**Use inheritance wisely**: Show abstract classes and their concrete subclasses (Vehicle → Car/Motorcycle). But don't create deep hierarchies — 2 levels is usually enough.
**Omit infrastructure details**: No database annotations, no Spring annotations in the diagram. Focus on domain design. The interviewer knows you'll add @Entity and @Service later.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The right level of detail in an LLD interview is all about showing your design decisions without wasting time on boilerplate. I'd include all the major classes — usually five to ten classes that each have a clear responsibility. For each class, I'd show three to five key attributes, the fields that actually matter for the business logic. Like in a parking lot system, I'd show that ParkingSpot has a vehicle type field and an occupied flag because those drive the assignment logic. But I wouldn't show created date or updated date fields — those are assumed. Same with methods: I'd include the important operations that show what each class does. For ParkingSpot, that's assign vehicle and release vehicle. I wouldn't draw get spot ID or set spot ID — every class has getters and setters, so showing them just wastes space. The relationships are critical. I'd definitely show composition with filled diamonds where one class owns another, like ParkingLot owns floors. I'd show inheritance where I'm using abstraction, like Vehicle being abstract with Car and Motorcycle subclasses. And I'd show interfaces if I'm using a pattern like Strategy for fee calculation. The common mistakes are either drawing just boxes with names and lines, which doesn't show any detail about what the classes contain, or going to the opposite extreme and trying to show every single field and method including constructors and all the getters. Both are wrong. You want the sweet spot: enough detail that someone could look at your diagram and understand the key design choices, but not so much that you run out of time or the board becomes unreadable. If I'm spending more than fifteen minutes drawing, I know I've gone too detailed.
